name: Takeo no Okusu (The Great Camphor of Takeo)
age_estimate: traditionally said to be about 3,000 years

location.address: 5335 Takeo, Takeo-cho, Takeo City, Saga Prefecture 843-0022, Japan (grounds of Takeo Shrine, along the maple-lined approach path beyond the main hall)

access: Free, no ticket. Stands on the open grounds of Takeo Shrine (a public Shinto shrine, founded 735 AD), reached along its own dedicated approach path (Momiji-dori) past a second hand-washing basin. Since a 2022 protective measure the no-entry perimeter around the trunk has been widened for the tree's own health, so visitors now view it from a short distance rather than approach the trunk itself; a 2024-2027 redevelopment of the neighbouring cultural hall does not close the tree to viewing.
transport: JR Takeo Onsen Station (Sasebo Line), about 25 minutes on foot; bus from the station toward Yutoku, alight at Takeo Koko-mae and walk about 10 minutes; about 10 minutes by car from Takeo-Kitakata IC on the Nagasaki Expressway.
verify_notes: Two independent sources, both official: Takeo City's own cultural-properties register page (designated a Takeo City Natural Monument, Plant, on 1970-07-15) and the Takeo City Tourism Association's own listing, which also carries a 2022-04-28 city notice about protective measures. Sacred tree (goshinboku) of Takeo Shrine; a stone hokora to Tenjin sits inside the trunk's hollow, which is roughly 12 tatami mats (about 20 sqm) across. Girth 20.0 m, height 30.0 m, canopy spread 30 m E-W by 33 m N-S, measured by the city. Tourism copy cites the Environment Agency's national giant-tree survey ranking it 7th in Japan by size; not independently checked against the survey's raw data, so treat as a repeated claim rather than a re-verified rank. AGE: the 3,000-year figure is temple/shrine tradition repeated by both official sources, not a ring count or growth-rate calculation; a camphor of this girth is dendrologically more often reckoned in the high hundreds to low thousands of years, so the wide age_min/age_max above reflects that this is a traditional figure rather than a scientific date. Flagged for that reason. ALIVE NOW: health has been visibly declining for years. City-led restoration ran 1994-2003 (soil work, cabling against splitting, corking removal and sealant in the hollow). An April 2022 city notice describes reduced foliage, dead major branches, spreading hollow decay and expanding dead sections of trunk, attributed to age and recent extreme weather, and widened the no-entry zone to prevent falling-branch accidents and let the roots recover; a 2025-dated search result confirms the tree is still standing and still viewable, with the wider closure a permanent-looking protective measure rather than a response to a new collapse. No report found of felling, death or removal. Would someone travel specifically for this tree: yes, it is one of the three trees named together as Saga Prefecture's largest ('全国最大級の巨木3選'), it anchors its own dedicated approach path within a historic shrine (founded 735 AD, its own listed structures), and it is a repeatedly cited candidate for one of Japan's largest trees by trunk girth. SUGGESTED PLACE: a new single-tree place named Takeo (not to be folded into the existing Kawago place, data/cities/kawago.json, kwg_001, which is a different camphor about 7.5 km away in Wakaki-cho within the same city and too far to share a walk). No id-prefix collision found for 'tak'. Second-source note: a geotagged Commons photo (File:Sacred_tree_'Takeo_no_Okusu'_of_Takeo_Shrine_1.jpg) carries a camera-location tag of 33.187581, 130.019317, within a few metres of the coordinate given in the brief, which is the tree-level confirmation behind location_precision: confirmed.
